title: Two Bugs That Hid in Plain Sight: A vLLM Debugging Detective Story — Asaf Gardin & Yuval Belfer
talk_summary: AI21 engineers debug two silent vLLM bugs (a scheduler calling decode before prefill on Mamba state, and a uint32 cache-index overflow) that produced confident gibberish only under load. The transferable core is their debugging methodology: fast reproduction via knob-tweaking, logprob comparison against a baseline framework, and threading request identity through opaque tensor pipelines.

takeaways.what_they_do: Run the same prompts through the suspect engine and a vanilla reference implementation, then compare per-token logprobs after softmax to localize where distributions diverge.

takeaways.technique: Reproduce under pressure, tweak knobs to change failure shape
takeaways.what_they_do: They shrank GPU memory and cranked rollouts-per-prompt to make a 1-in-1000 bug fire on step 1, then used knobs that change *how* it fails, not just how often.
takeaways.evidence_quote: we wanted to find some lever that changes how things fail and not just how much they fail
takeaways.numbers: bug went from every 12 steps to step 1 at 128 rollouts/prompt

takeaways.technique: Thread request identity through opaque stages
takeaways.what_they_do: They injected a request ID into the forward-context object and propagated it down to the kernels so they could breakpoint on the exact bad request and inspect its metadata.

takeaways.technique: Beware resource-pressure fixes that mask bugs
takeaways.what_they_do: Shrinking GPU memory made the overflow bug disappear because the buffer never grew large enough to wrap — a 'fix' that hid the defect.

takeaways.technique: Silent failures lie confidently — distrust high-confidence output
takeaways.what_they_do: They frame the class of bug as one with no crash, no warning, high confidence, bad output, and argue stateful systems 'lie to you confidently'.
